pages.name: Embarking and Departure
pages.html:
When the spacers accept a job, they may prepare to leave. The following procedure is the typical procedure of any starship.

  • Multiple Jobs: Typically, a spacer will take on multiple jobs and sort out the order in which to do them. They can also take on passengers heading in their direction for additional income, or transport freight cargo and mail to the next location if there is room in the cargo bay.

A) Prepare for Departure: Takes 1D hours Total

  • 1) Load cargo: List the items and tonnage of each group of cargo onto the manifest.
  • 2) Load low-berth passengers: List names and destination onto the manifest.
  • 3) Load other passengers: List names and destination onto the manifest.
  • 4) Load courier cargo: List tonnage of mail onto the manifest.
  • 5) Collect payment from all non-low-berth passengers.
  • 6) Refuel: 500cr per tonne for refined or 100cr for unrefined (-2 DM to Astrogation checks).

B) Departure: Takes 1Dx10 Minutes Per Skill Check to secure and initiate departure from a starport.

  • 1) Lift off and achieve orbit: Only make a Pilot check if taking off in hazardous or dangerous circumstances.
  • 2) Set course to destination: Either a jump point or location within the system. This can take days of travel.
  • 3) Scan area for encounters per day: Roll 1D, a 6+ is an encounter. Some areas may have more or less frequent encounters. See pg. 80 for more information
  • 4) Prepare to jump.

C) Jump Space

  • Onboard events: Referee determines if any events occur onboard.
  • Spacers roleplay what they are doing during their time onboard. Examples are downtime activities like repairs, studying, training, etc.
  • After a week passes, the ship leaves jump space.

D) Arrival in Star System

  • Make contact with destination: Sensor operator contacts the destination.
  • Scan area for encounters per day of intra-system travel.
  • Achieve orbit and dock: Only make a Pilot check if taking off in hazardous or dangerous circumstances.

E) Complete Arrival: Takes a Total of 1D Hours to deal with customs and unload any passengers and cargo.

  • 1) Customs: The ship captain/owner/ or anyone with the highest SOC reports the manifest and negotiates/pay duties as needed.
  • 2) Pay docking fees and additional expenses: Broker Check Average (8+) to negotiate lower payment.
  • 3) Unload passengers (If any).
  • 4) Unload mail (If any).
  • 5) Unload cargo (if any).
  • 6) Unload low-berth passengers (If any).

F) Shore Leave

  • Report job completion: If the spacers have just completed the terms of a haired job, they must check in to finalize the job. For trade and transportation, this is normally a port of call to a computer terminal or port authority, but completing other jobs, the referee may have them follow through with a specific NPC. Once this is done, the spacers can receive their payout.
  • Crew members perform any necessary routines: Crew members with specific rolls that have activities planned while docked are expected to do them before next departure as the referee determines. Examples of crew positions and their responsibilities can be found on the Crew Position table on pg. 70 for more information.
  • Encounters: Typically, every six hours spent in a location away from the ship exploring an environment, an encounter will be rolled. By default, an encounter represents the spacers noticing something happening within their vicinity. See Starport Encounters on pg. 60-61 for more information.
  • Take on a new job: The spacers may choose to find new patrons or other employment in the new location they are docked.
  • Downtime activities: Spacers can engage in downtime activities, see Downtime Table for more.

pages.name: Manifest
pages.html:
The ship will have a manifest of all of the contents on the ship, which will be approved for departure and then reviewed upon arrival at your destination.

  • On Departure: The duty officer at your departing location will review the manifest and sign off on it.
  • On Arrival: The duty officer at your destination will review the approved manifest to make sure everything is accounted for.
  • Discrepancies in the Manifest: If the spacer’s manifest is incorrect, they will be subjected to paying customs per discrepancy found. The following table lists the amount owed upon arrival, by starport type. If the spacers are not docking at a starport, then roll 1D to determine the equivalent costs for customs: 1) A 2) B 3) C 4) D 5-6) E. No customs are collected at Starport X due to a lack of infrastructure. The amount of credits owed is per person/crew member or per ton of cargo.

pages.name: The Vast Size of Space
pages.html:
The scale of space is immense and mostly empty. Star systems are light years away from each other, making travel only possible with faster-than-light travel. This also means information only travels as far as the fastest ship, meaning that news will take longer to reach further areas.

Book p.67

pages.name: Interplanetary Travel
pages.html:
Interplanetary travel is intra-system space travel by ships that travel locally to neighbouring planets, satellites, and colonies within the same star system. Interplanetary travel is made using a ship's Maneuver Drive, or M-Drive, which represents the main propulsion systems for a ship.

pages.name: Interstellar Travel
pages.html:
Interstellar travel is travelling the vast void between star systems. Interstellar travel is made using a jump-drive, which provides a starship the means to slip through spacetime travelling faster than light.

  • Jump time: Jumping takes one week of time to jump regardless of the jump rating.
  • Jump distance: The amount of distance covered is determined in parsecs, where the Jump rating equals the parsecs travelled.

Example: A J-2 rating means the ship can travel two parsecs in one jump.

Book p.67

pages.name: Example of One Month of Spacing
pages.html:
Example of One Month of a Spacer Hauling Trade Goods

Working starships typically make two jumps a month.

  • Week 1: Starport and interplanetary travel: A ship owner makes payments for their ship’s mortgage and maintenance and finds jobs to perform. Then they travel from the starport to space and head to the jump point.
  • Week 2: Enter, travel through, and exit ump-space.
  • Week 3: Travel to destination, land, unload, and pay fees. Find more work then travel back into space.
  • Week 4: Enter, travel through, and exit jump-pace.

Book p.67

pages.name: Travelling to a Jump Point
pages.html:
The Jump Point Travel table at the bottom of the page is designed to help determine how much time is needed to travel from a planet’s orbit to a calculated jump point.

  • Jump point distance: All jump points must be at least 100x the planet’s diametre away from a planet; otherwise the gravity of a planet might pull a ship out of jump-space and fling them in an unwanted direction.
  • Travel time to jump point: All time below is calculated based on a starship’s M-Drive rating. The time is rounded to the nearest quarter-hour for simplification.
  • Planet Code: The number indicated on the leftmost column is determined by the universal world code of the planet. See World Generation on pg. 70 for more information.
